newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Two rivals concede poll victory to Liberia's Taylor.
newsitem.headline: Two rivals concede poll victory to Liberia's Taylor.

text.p: Two candidates in Liberia's presidential election conceded on Wednesday that they had lost to former warlord Charles Taylor who has taken an insurmountable lead in partial results.
As electoral chiefs made final ballot checks before proclaiming Taylor winner in Saturday's elections, his rivals Cletus Wortorson and Baccus Mathews bowed out to Taylor.

Their declarations were the first signs that political leaders in the faction-ridden counrty were heeding calls from donors to accept the results of the elections intended to wrap up a regional peace plan on ending seven years of civil war.

Two other former warlords and Taylor rivals for president -- Alhaji Kromah and George Boley -- have not reacted to the latest results announced on Tuesday night, although Kromah earlier alleged poll malpractice.

Taylor's closest rival, former United Nations Ellen Johnson- Sirleaf, the only woman among 12 presidential candidates, on Tuesday renewed charges of poll irregularities but reserved judgment on the credibility of the election.
"Results of the elections announced so far show that the Liberian people overwhelmingly decided that Taylor should be the president of Liberia," Wortorson told reporters.
Wortoson, 60, came fourth with 2.5 percent of votes in the latest partial results showing Taylor with more than 75 percent with three-quarters of votes counted.

"We congratulate Mr Taylor," said Wortorson, an engineer and administrator. He showed initial electoral promise because of his popularity during a stint as deputy chairman of the National Football Association in the soccer-mad country.
Calling on his Alliance of Political Parties supporters to support Taylor, Wortoson said: "I intend to cooperate with Mr Taylor" in the task of rebuilding a war-shattered country.
Mathews, a former foreign minister, also endorsed the elections as "reasonably free and fair". He called on Taylor's other rivals alleging malpractice to accept the results.
"There were problems but they were not massive enough to affect the result," Mathews told Reuters.
"It's much easier for me to accept these results and go beyond them," said Mathews, a campaigner for multi-party democracy dating back to one-party rule in the 1970s.
Elections commission chairman Henry Andrews told a news conference he hoped to formally announce the winner by Wednesday night -- certainly not later than Thursday, by law.
He said Taylor had not been proclaimed the winner after Tuesday's results as the commission wanted to be sure turnout was as it estimated -- 600,000 from 700,000 registered voters.
Taylor needed 50 percent plus to win on the first round.
Taylor put back a scheduled Wednesday news conference to Thursday, but aides gave no reason for the change.
Liberians looking for strong leadership after an agonising seven-year civil war voted overwhelmingly on Saturday for the man who started the fighting.
The conduct of the presidential and general elections, Liberia's first since 1985, received unanimous endorsement from more than 500 foreign monitors and over 1,000 local observers.

The elections had a special significance for Liberians, taking place almost on the eve on July 26 of the 150th birthday of the country founded by freed American slaves in 1847 as Africa's first modern republic.

They also wrap up a civil war peace accord engineered by the the 16-nation Economic Community of West African States. Troops from the regional peacekeeping force ECOMOG have been policing Liberia since 1992 and provided security for the poll.
